tasks.description: Define a function `greet(name)` that returns 'Hello, {name}!'. Call it with 'World' and print the result.
tasks.hint:
`def` defines a function, `return` sends a value back to the caller.
`def greet(name): return f'Hello, {name}!'`
Then call and print: `print(greet('World'))` — calling without print would compute but show nothing.
tasks.walkthrough:
The function takes one parameter and builds a greeting with an f-string.
`return` hands the greeting back, so the call `greet('World')` turns into the string, and `print` shows it.

tasks.description: Define a function `add(a, b)` that returns the sum of two numbers. Call it with 3 and 5, print the result.
tasks.hint:
Parameters `a` and `b` are like local variables that receive the values you pass in.
`def add(a, b): return a + b`
Calling `add(3, 5)` sets `a=3` and `b=5`, then returns `8`.
tasks.walkthrough:
When `add(3, 5)` runs, `a` becomes 3 and `b` becomes 5 inside the function.
The sum is returned and printed.

tasks.description: Define a function `is_even(n)` that returns True if n is even, False if not. Test it with 7 and print the result.
tasks.hint:
`n % 2` gives the remainder: `0` for even numbers, `1` for odd numbers.
You can return the expression directly — no need for an if/else:
`return n % 2 == 0` evaluates to True or False automatically.
tasks.walkthrough:
`n % 2 == 0` is already a True/False value, so it can be returned directly.
There's no need for `if ... return True else return False`.
7 leaves a remainder of 1, so the comparison is False.

tasks.description: Define a function `power(base, exp=2)` where exp has a default value of 2. Call power(5) and print the result.
tasks.hint:
Default parameters are set in the `def` signature: `def power(base, exp=2):`
If the caller doesn't pass `exp`, Python uses `2` automatically.
`power(5)` → `5 ** 2` → `25`; `power(5, 3)` → `5 ** 3` → `125`
tasks.walkthrough:
`exp=2` in the def line is a default. Calling `power(5)` with one argument uses that default.
5 to the power of 2 is 25. Calling `power(5, 3)` would override the default and give 125.

tasks.description: Define a function `min_max(numbers)` that takes a list and returns both the minimum and maximum as a tuple. Call it with [3, 1, 7, 2, 9] and print both values.
tasks.hint:
Python's `min()` and `max()` find the smallest and largest values in a sequence.
Return two values separated by a comma: `return min(numbers), max(numbers)` — Python packs them into a tuple.
Unpack when calling: `lo, hi = min_max([3,1,7,2,9])` then `print(lo, hi)`
tasks.walkthrough:
Returning two values separated by a comma packs them into a tuple.
`lo, hi = ...` unpacks that tuple into two variables.
`print(lo, hi)` prints them separated by a space, giving `1 9`.

tasks.description: Define a function `repeat_print(text, times)` that prints text on separate lines, times number of times. Call it with 'hello' and 3.
tasks.hint:
Use `for _ in range(times):` inside the function (the `_` means 'I don't use this variable').
Each iteration calls `print(text)` once.
Calling `repeat_print('hello', 3)` should print 'hello' three times.
tasks.walkthrough:
The loop runs `times` times. The underscore is a conventional name for a loop variable you don't use.
This function prints rather than returns, because the task is about producing output, so calling it is enough.

tasks.description: Define a function `celsius_to_fahrenheit(c)` that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit. Formula: F = c * 9/5 + 32. Call it with 100 and print the result.
tasks.hint:
Translate the formula directly: `return c * 9/5 + 32`
`9/5` in Python is `1.8` (a float), so the result will be a float.
`celsius_to_fahrenheit(100)` → `212.0`
tasks.walkthrough:
The formula is typed in almost exactly as written in the task.
`9 / 5` is 1.8, a float, so the whole result is a float: 212.0.

lesson.intro:
A function is a named block of code you can run whenever you want, as many times
as you want. You've been using them all week: `print`, `len`, `input`. Today you
write your own. It's the single biggest step towards programs that don't turn into
a wall of repeated lines.

sections.heading: Defining and calling
sections.body:
`def` starts a definition, then the name, then brackets, then a colon.
The indented block is the body. Nothing in the body runs until you call
the function by writing its name with brackets.
sections.code:
def say_hi():
    print('Hi there')

say_hi()
say_hi()

sections.heading: Parameters: giving the function something to work with
sections.body:
Names inside the brackets of the `def` are parameters. When you call the
function, the values you pass fill them in. Inside the body they're just
ordinary variables.

sections.heading: return: sending a value back
sections.body:
Printing inside a function is fine for now, but usually you want the function
to hand a result back so the caller decides what to do with it. That's `return`.
The moment `return` runs, the function ends.

A function that returns something doesn't show anything on its own. You still
have to `print` the result, or store it.
sections.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(3, 5)
print(result)
print(add(10, 20))

sections.heading: Default values
sections.body:
A parameter can have a default, written with `=` in the `def` line. If the
caller leaves it out, the default is used.
sections.code:
def power(base, exp=2):
    return base ** exp

print(power(5))
print(power(5, 3))

sections.heading: Returning more than one thing
sections.body:
Separate the values with commas after `return`. Python bundles them into a
tuple, and you can unpack them straight into two variables.

watch_out: Defining a function but never calling it. The `def` block only describes what to do.
Calling `add(3, 5)` on its own line and wondering why nothing appears. Wrap it in `print()`.
Mixing up `print` and `return`. `print` shows a value; `return` hands it back to whoever called the function.
Anything after a `return` in the same block never runs.
